title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Coming back from church service, Alexey Alexandrovitch had spent the whole morning indoors. He had two pieces of business to deal with: first, to receive and send on a deputation from the native tribes that was on its way to Petersburg and was now in Moscow; second, to write the promised letter to the lawyer. The deputation, although it had been summoned at Alexey Alexandrovitch's instigation, had its uncomfortable, even dangerous side, and he was glad he had found it in Moscow. Its members had not the faintest grasp of their duty or the part they were meant to play. They naively believed it was their job to set out their needs and the actual conditions on the ground before the commission and to ask the government for help, and quite failed to grasp that some of their statements and requests supported the opposing side's case and so spoiled the whole business. Alexey Alexandrovitch worked with them at length, drew up a program from which they were not to depart, and after sending them off wrote a letter to Petersburg to guide the deputation there. His chief ally in the affair was Countess Lidia Ivanovna. She was a specialist in deputations, and no one knew better than she did how to manage them and steer them in the right direction. Having finished with that, Alexey Alexandrovitch wrote the letter to the lawyer. Without the slightest hesitation he gave him a free hand to act as he thought best. With the letter he enclosed three of Vronsky's notes to Anna, which he had taken from her portfolio.

Ever since Alexey Alexandrovitch had left home meaning never to return to his family, and since he had been to the lawyer's and spoken about his intention, if only to one man, and especially since he had transferred the matter from real life into the world of ink and paper, he had grown more and more accustomed to his decision, and could now clearly see how it was to be carried out.
He was sealing the envelope to the lawyer when he heard Stepan Arkadyevitch's loud voice. Stepan Arkadyevitch was arguing with Alexey Alexandrovitch's servant and insisting on being announced.
"No matter," Alexey Alexandrovitch thought, "so much the better. I'll tell him at once where I stand with regard to his sister, and explain why I can't dine with him."
"Show him in!" he said aloud, gathering up his papers and tucking them into the blotter.

"There, you see — you're talking nonsense, and he's at home!" came Stepan Arkadyevitch's voice, addressed to the servant who had refused to let him in; pulling off his coat as he came, Oblonsky walked into the room. "Well, I'm awfully glad I've caught you! So I trust...." Stepan Arkadyevitch began cheerfully.
"I cannot come," Alexey Alexandrovitch said coldly, standing and not asking his visitor to sit down.

Alexey Alexandrovitch had meant to step at once into those frigid relations he ought to maintain with the brother of a wife against whom he was bringing a divorce suit. But he had not reckoned with the ocean of kindliness brimming in Stepan Arkadyevitch's heart.
Stepan Arkadyevitch's clear, shining eyes opened wide.
"Why can't you? What do you mean?" he asked, bewildered, in French. "Oh, but it's a promise. And we're all counting on you."
"I want to tell you that I cannot dine at your house, because the relationship that has existed between us must end."
"How? What do you mean? What for?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling.
"Because I am beginning a divorce suit against your sister, my wife. I should have...."
But before Alexey Alexandrovitch could finish his sentence, Stepan Arkadyevitch behaved in a way he had not at all expected. He groaned and sank into an armchair.
"No, Alexey Alexandrovitch! What are you saying?" Oblonsky cried, and the pain showed in his face.
"It is so."
"Forgive me, I can't, I can't believe it!"

Alexey Alexandrovitch sat down, sensing that his words had not had the effect he expected, and that he would have to explain his position, and that no matter what he said, his relationship with his brother-in-law would not really change.
"Yes, I have been driven to the painful necessity of seeking a divorce," he said.

"I will say just one thing, Alexey Alexandrovitch. I know you to be an excellent, upright man; I know Anna — forgive me, I cannot change my opinion of her — to be a good, an excellent woman; and so, forgive me, I cannot believe it. There must be some misunderstanding," he said.
"Oh, if it were only a misunderstanding!..."
"Pardon, I understand," Stepan Arkadyevitch broke in. "But of course.... One thing: you must not act in haste. You must not, you must not act in haste!"
"I am not acting in haste," Alexey Alexandrovitch said coldly, "but one cannot ask anyone for advice in such a matter. I have made up my mind completely."

"This is awful!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "There is one thing I would beg you to do, Alexey Alexandrovitch. I beseech you, do it!" he said. "No action has been taken yet, if I understand rightly. Before you go to your lawyer, see my wife, talk to her. She loves Anna like a sister, she loves you, and she's a wonderful woman. For God's sake, talk with her! Do me that favor, I beg you!"
Alexey Alexandrovitch thought, and Stepan Arkadyevitch watched him sympathetically, not breaking his silence.
"You will go and see her?"
"I don't know. That's just why I haven't been over. I think our relations must change."

"Why should they? I don't see it. Allow me to think that, apart from our family connection, you have for me, at least in part, the same friendly feeling I have always had for you ... and a sincere respect," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, pressing his hand. "Even if your worst suspicions were correct, I don't — and never would — take it upon myself to judge either side, and I see no reason why our relations should suffer. But now, do this — come and see my wife."
"Well, we see the matter differently," Alexey Alexandrovitch said coldly. "However, we won't go into it."

"No; why shouldn't you come to dinner today anyway? My wife is expecting you. Please, do come. And above all, talk it over with her. She's a wonderful woman. For God's sake, on my knees, I implore you!"
"If you wish it so much, I'll come," said Alexey Alexandrovitch with a sigh.

And, eager to change the subject, he asked about something that interested them both — the new head of Stepan Arkadyevitch's department, a man not yet old, who had suddenly been promoted to such a high position.

Alexey Alexandrovitch had never cared for Count Anitchkin and had always disagreed with him on policy. But now, from a feeling familiar enough among officials — the hatred a man passed over for promotion feels for the one promoted ahead of him — he could not stand him.
"Well, have you seen him?" said Alexey Alexandrovitch with a malicious smile.
"Of course; he was at our meeting yesterday. He seems to know his job thoroughly and to be very energetic."

"Yes, but what is his energy aimed at?" Alexey Alexandrovitch said. "Is he trying to accomplish anything, or only to undo what's been done? It's the great misfortune of our government — this paper administration of which he is a worthy representative."

"Really, I don't know what fault one could find with him. I don't know his policies, but one thing I do know — he's a very nice fellow," Stepan Arkadyevitch said. "I've just been with him, and he really is a capital fellow. We lunched together, and I taught him how to make — you know that drink, wine and oranges. It's so cooling. It's amazing he didn't know it. He took to it like anything. No, really, he's a capital fellow."
Stepan Arkadyevitch glanced at his watch.
"Why, good heavens, it's already four, and I still have to call on Dolgovushin! So please do come round for dinner. You can't imagine how you will hurt my wife and me."
The way Alexey Alexandrovitch saw his brother-in-law out was very different from the way he had received him.
"I've promised, and I'll come," he answered wearily.
"Believe me, I appreciate it, and I hope you won't regret it," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, smiling.
And, pulling on his coat as he went, he patted the footman on the head, chuckled, and went out.
"Five o'clock, and not evening dress, please!" he shouted once more, turning at the door.
